draft.title: Exothermic and endothermic reactions
card: Chemical reactions involve energy changes. Often this energy moves as heat between the reaction and its surroundings.
a reaction that releases energy to its surroundings, so they get warmer. Burning wood is an example.
a reaction that takes in energy from its surroundings, so they get cooler. An instant ice pack is an example.
A thermometer in the surroundings shows which kind it is. A temperature rise means exothermic. A temperature fall means endothermic.
draft.remember: Exothermic: energy out, surroundings warm. Endothermic: energy in, surroundings cool.

a.q: Which description fits an exothermic reaction?
opts: It releases energy and warms its surroundings
It takes in energy and cools its surroundings
It releases energy and cools its surroundings
It takes in energy and warms its surroundings
a.why: An exothermic reaction gives out energy, so the surroundings gain energy and get warmer. The option about taking in energy describes an endothermic reaction, where the surroundings lose energy and cool.
a.clue: Think of burning: where does the heat go?

b.q: Priya mixes two powders in a cup of water. The thermometer reading falls from 22 °C to 14 °C. What does this show about the reaction?
opts: It is endothermic because it took in energy
It is exothermic because it took in energy
It is exothermic because the water got colder
It is endothermic because it released energy
b.why: The surroundings cooled, so energy moved from them into the reaction. That makes it endothermic. The tempting mistake is to link cold with exothermic, but exothermic reactions warm their surroundings.
b.clue: Look at what happened to the surroundings, not the reaction.

a.best: It releases energy and warms its surroundings

b.best: It is endothermic because it took in energy

problems.detail: Most instant ice packs work by dissolving a salt such as ammonium nitrate in water. Point 1 calls dissolving a physical change, so calling the ice pack a 'reaction' clashes with that point. The chapter outline uses the same example, so the owner may accept it, but it could confuse students. Calling it an endothermic 'process' or 'change' would avoid the clash.

Why (a) refers to 'the option about taking in energy', but two options mention taking in energy. One of them ('takes in energy and warms its surroundings') does not describe an endothermic reaction. Why (a) also says nothing about the 'releases energy and cools' distractor.

check.summary: Both questions are sound, each with one clear right answer. Minor issues: the instant ice pack example is usually dissolving, which point 1 calls a physical change, and Why (a) refers vaguely to 'the option about taking in energy' when two options mention it.
